name: Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Syndrome

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical diagnostic criteria for Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Syndrome

criteria.description: Preaxial polydactyly of hands or feet
Cutaneous or osseous syndactyly (fusion of digits)
Identification of pathogenic GLI3 gene mutation
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of macrocephaly plus either preaxial polydactyly or syndactyly, or identification of a pathogenic GLI3 mutation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing for GLI3 mutations can confirm diagnosis but is not always necessary if clinical criteria are met.

imaging: Radiographs showing preaxial polydactyly and syndactyly
Brain MRI may show corpus callosum hypoplasia or hydrocephalus
genetic: Pathogenic variants in GLI3 gene (autosomal dominant inheritance)
other: Family history consistent with autosomal dominant pattern
Physical examination revealing characteristic craniofacial and limb anomalies

distinguishingFeatures: More severe central nervous system malformations
Extra digits located on the ulnar/fibular side rather than preaxial

redFlags: Rapidly increasing head circumference suggesting hydrocephalus
Signs of respiratory distress due to airway anomalies
references: Orphanet Report Series: Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Syndrome (ORPHA:380)
Biesecker LG. Greig syndrome. In: GeneReviews® [Internet]. University of Washington, Seattle; 1993-2024.
commonPitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as isolated polydactyly or syndactyly without recognizing the craniofacial features.
Craniosynostosis may be subtle and overlooked, leading to missed diagnosis.
Confused with other syndromes featuring polydactyly, such as Pallister-Hall syndrome, due to overlapping limb anomalies.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: Absence of hypothalamic hamartoma and imperforate anus in Greig Cephalopolysyndactyly Syndrome.
Presence of preaxial polydactyly (thumb/big toe side) and craniofacial anomalies in GCPS, not seen in isolated postaxial polydactyly.
GCPS lacks the severe syndactyly (mitten hand) and intellectual disability commonly seen in Apert syndrome.

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of preaxial polydactyly or syndactyly of hands/feet.
No evidence of craniofacial anomalies such as macrocephaly or hypertelorism.
Presence of hypothalamic hamartoma (suggests Pallister-Hall syndrome instead).
